Dispersive Blow-up for Solutions of the Zakharov-Kuznetsov equation

F. Linares Address:  IMPA
Estrada Dona Castorina 110
Rio de Janeiro 22460-320, RJ Brasil Email address: linares@impa.br , A. Pastor Address: IMECC-UNICAMP, Rua Sérgio Buarque de Holanda, 651, 13083-859, Campinas-SP, Brazil Email address: apastor@ime.unicamp.br and J. Drumond Silva Address: Center for Mathematical Analysis, Geometry and Dynamical Systems,Department of Mathematics, Instituto Superior Técnico, Universidade de Lisboa, Av. Rovisco Pais, 1049-001 Lisboa, Portugal Email address: jsilva@math.tecnico.ulisboa.pt
Abstract.

The main purpose here is the study of dispersive blow-up for solutions of the Zakharov-Kuznetsov equation. Dispersive blow-up refers to point singularities due to the focusing of short or long waves. We will construct initial data such that solutions of the linear problem present this kind of singularities. Then we show that the corresponding solutions of the nonlinear problem present dispersive blow-up inherited from the linear component part of the equation. Similar results are obtained for the generalized Zakharov-Kuznetsov equation.

Key words and phrases: 
Nonlinear dispersive equations; Zakharov-Kuznetsov equation; Dispersive Blow-up
2010 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary: 35Q53. Secondary: 35B44

1. Introduction

In this paper we consider solutions of the initial value problem (IVP) associated to the two dimensional Zakharov-Kuznetsov (ZK) and generalized Zakharov-Kuznetsov (gZK) equations, respectively k=1k=1 and k≥2k\geq 2,

(1.1) {∂tu+∂xΔu+uk∂xu=0,(x,y)∈ℝ2,t∈ℝ,k∈ℤ+,u⁡(x,y,0)=u0​(x,y)\begin{cases}\partial_{t}u+\partial_{x}\Delta u+u^{k}\partial_{x}u=0,\quad(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{2},\,t\in\mathbb{R},k\in\mathbb{Z}^{+},\\ u(x,y,0)=u_{0}(x,y)\end{cases}

where uu is a real function and Δ\Delta denotes the Laplace operator in space variables.

The equation above, for k=1k=1, arises in the context of plasma physics, where it was formally derived by Zakharov and Kuznetsov [35] as a long wave small-amplitude limit of the Euler-Poisson system in the “cold plasma” approximation. This formal long-wave limit was rigorously justified by Lannes, Linares and Saut in [22] (see also [15] for derivation in a different context).

The Zakharov-Kuznetsov equation can be seen as a natural multi-dimensional extension of the Korteweg-de Vries (KdV) equation, quite different from the well-known Kadomtsev-Petviashvili (KP) equation which is obtained as an asymptotic model of various nonlinear dispersive systems under a different scaling.

Contrary to the Korteweg-de Vries or the Kadomtsev-Petviashvili equations, the Zakharov-Kuznetsov equation is not completely integrable but it has a Hamiltonian structure and possesses three invariants, namely,

I⁡(t)=∫ℝ2u⁡(x,y,t)​𝑑x​𝑑y=∫ℝ2u0​(x,y)​𝑑x​𝑑y=I⁡(0),I(t)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}u(x,y,t)\,dxdy=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}u_{0}(x,y)\,dxdy=I(0),
M⁡(t)=∫ℝ2u2​(x,y,t)​𝑑x​𝑑y=∫ℝ2u02​(x,y)​𝑑x​𝑑y=M⁡(0),M(t)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}u^{2}(x,y,t)\,dxdy=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}u_{0}^{2}(x,y)\,dxdy=M(0),

and

E⁡(t)=12​∫ℝ2(|∇u|2−u33)​𝑑x​𝑑y=12​∫ℝ2(|∇u0|2−u033)​𝑑x​𝑑y=E⁡(0).E(t)=\frac{1}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\Big(|\nabla u|^{2}-\frac{u^{3}}{3}\Big)dxdy=\frac{1}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\Big(|\nabla u_{0}|^{2}-\frac{u_{0}^{3}}{3}\Big)dxdy=E(0).

Regarding the well-posedness for the IVP (1.1) when k=1k=1, the best local result available in the literature was recently obtained by Kinoshita [21] for initial data in Hs​(ℝ2)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{2}), for s>−1/4s>-1/4, and using the conserved quantities above global well-posedness is established in Hs​(ℝ2)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{2}), s≥0s\geq 0. Previous results include those by Molinet and Pilod [31], Grünrock and Herr [13], Faminskii [9] and Linares and Pastor [25].

In the case of the generalized Zakharov-Kuznetsov equation (gZK), i.e. (1.1) for k≥2k\geq 2, we shall briefly describe what is known for the well-posedness of the associated IVP. In the 2D case, the scale argument suggests local well-posedness results for data in Hs​(ℝ2)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{2}), for s>sk=1−2/ks>s_{k}=1-2/k. Sharp local results were obtained by Ribaud and Vento [34], for k≥4k\geq 4. In [12], Grünrock proved the local well-posedness in H˙sk​(ℝn)\dot{H}^{s_{k}}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) for n=2,3n=2,3 and sk=n/2−2/ks_{k}=n/2-2/k. For the particular nonlinearity k=2k=2, also called modified Zakharov-Kuznetsov equation (mZK), for which L2​(ℝ2)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) is the critical space suggested by the scaling argument, local well-posedness was shown for data in Hs​(ℝ2)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{2}), for s≥1/4s\geq 1/4 in [34]. Still for the nonlinearity k=2k=2 global well-posedness in Hs​(ℝ2)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{2}), s>53/63s>53/63, for initial data with suitable L2L^{2} norm, was established by Linares and Pastor in [26]. Recently, this Sobolev index was pushed down to s>3/4s>3/4 by Bhattacharya, Farah, and Roudenko in [2].

Here our main goal is to establish a dispersive blow-up result for solutions of the IVP associated to the ZK and gZK equations. We recall that the notion of dispersive singularity was first addressed in [1] (see also [5]) for solutions of the linear Korteweg-de Vries equation,

∂tu+∂xu+∂x3u=0,x∈ℝ,t∈ℝ.\partial_{t}u+\partial_{x}u+\partial_{x}^{3}u=0,\hskip 15.0ptx\in\mathbb{R},\,t\in\mathbb{R}.

Roughly, it is possible to obtain a solution u=u⁡(x,t)u=u(x,t) that blows up in the L∞L^{\infty}-norm in finite time by considering an infinitely smooth, bounded initial wave profile u​(x,0)=u0​(x)u(x,0)=u_{0}(x), possessing finite energy. Moreover, the blow-up point (x∗,t∗)(x^{*},t^{*}) can be specified arbitrarily in the upper-half plane ℝ×(0,∞)\mathbb{R}\times(0,\infty). In [4] Bona and Saut started the mathematical analysis of the dispersive blow-up for solutions of the nonlinear generalized KdV equation. More precisely, they proved the following:

Theorem A ([4]).

Let T>0T>0 be given and let {(xn,tn)}n=1∞\{(x_{n},t_{n})\}_{n=1}^{\infty} be a sequence of points in ℝ×(0,T)\mathbb{R}\times(0,T) without finite limit points and such that {tn}n=1∞\{t_{n}\}_{n=1}^{\infty} is bounded below by a positive constant. Let either s=0s=0 and k=1k=1 or s≥2s\geq 2 and k≥1k\geq 1 be an arbitrary integer. Then there exists ψ∈Hs​(ℝ)∩C∞​(ℝ)\psi\in H^{s}(\mathbb{R})\cap C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}) such that the solution of the IVP

{ut+∂x3u+uk​∂xu=0,u⁡(x,0)=ψ⁡(x),\begin{cases}u_{t}+\partial_{x}^{3}u+u^{k}\partial_{x}u=0,\\ u(x,0)=\psi(x),\end{cases}

satisfies

  1. (1)

    uu lies in L∞​([0,T]:Hs​(ℝ))∩L2​([0,T]:Hlocs+1​(ℝ))L^{\infty}([0,T]:H^{s}(\mathbb{R}))\cap L^{2}([0,T]:H^{s+1}_{\rm loc}(\mathbb{R})), or in C⁡([0,T]:Hs​(ℝ))∩L2​([0,T]:Hlocs+1​(ℝ))C([0,T]:H^{s}(\mathbb{R}))\cap L^{2}([0,T]:H^{s+1}_{\rm loc}(\mathbb{R})), if s≥2s\geq 2.

  2. (2)

    ∂xsu\partial_{x}^{s}u is continuous on ℝ×(0,T)\∪n=1∞{(xn,tn)}\mathbb{R}\times(0,T)\backslash\cup_{n=1}^{\infty}\{(x_{n},t_{n})\}, and

  3. (3)

    lim(x,t)→(xn,tn)​∂xsu⁡(x,t)=+∞\underset{(x,t)\to(x_{n},t_{n})}{\lim}\partial_{x}^{s}u(x,t)=+\infty, for n=1,2,…n=1,2,\dots.

The main idea behind the proof is to show that the Duhamel term associated to the solution of the IVP is smoother than the linear term of the solution. In [30] Linares and Scialom obtained the result above, for k≥2k\geq 2, by employing the smoothing effect properties without using weighted Sobolev spaces. Recently, Linares, Ponce and Smith [29] improved the previous result using fractional weighted spaces in the case k=1k=1, i.e., for the KdV equation (see also [24]).

Analogous phenomena also appear in other linear dispersive equations, such as the linear Schrödinger equation and the free surface water waves system linearized around the rest state [5]. In [5] Bona and Saut constructed initial data with point singularities for solutions of the linear Schrödinger equation. Bona, Ponce, Saut and Sparber [3] established the dispersive blow-up for the semilinear Schrödinger equation in dimension nn and other Schrödinger type equations. Simplifications of the proof and low regularity requirements were given in [14]. The main tools employed to show these results were the intrinsic smoothing effects of these dispersive equations. We remark that this is the only known result up to date regarding dispersive blow-up in n>1n>1 dimensions.

In order to state and prove our results we will exploit the symmetric form of (1.1). We recall that the linear change of variables introduced by Grünrock and Herr in [13], i.e.,

x′=μ​x+λ​y,y′=μ​x−λ​y,x^{\prime}=\mu x+\lambda y,\,\,\,y^{\prime}=\mu x-\lambda y,

with μ=4−1/3,λ=3μ\mu=4^{-1/3},\lambda=\sqrt{3}\mu, symmetrizes the equation so that the IVP (1.1) can be written as

(1.2) {∂tv+∂x3v+∂y3v+4−1/3(vk∂xv+vk∂yv)=0,(x,y)∈ℝ2,t∈ℝ,v⁡(x,y,0)=v0​(x,y).\begin{cases}\partial_{t}v+\partial_{x}^{3}v+\partial_{y}^{3}v+4^{-1/3}(v^{k}\partial_{x}v+v^{k}\partial_{y}v)=0,\enskip(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{2},t\in\mathbb{R},\\ v(x,y,0)=v_{0}(x,y).\end{cases}

This allows us to consider the IVP (1.2) instead of (1.1) without changing the well-posedness theory. One of the reasons to work with this symmetric equation is that we obtain better Strichartz estimates (see Lemma 2.1) which will be key in our argument. Besides, some technical issues are easier to deal with in the symmetrized equation, as we will explain below.

The integral form of the solution of (1.2) then becomes (we drop the unimportant constant 4−1/34^{-1/3})

(1.3) v⁡(t)=V⁡(t)​v0−∫0tV⁡(t−t′)​vk​(∂xv+∂yv)​(t′)​d​t′,v(t)=V(t)v_{0}-\int_{0}^{t}V(t-t^{\prime})v^{k}(\partial_{x}v+\partial_{y}v)(t^{\prime})\,dt^{\prime},

where V⁡(t)V(t) is the unitary group associated to the symmetric linear problem

(1.4) {∂tv+∂x3v+∂y3v=0,v⁡(x,y,0)=v0​(x,y),\begin{cases}\partial_{t}v+\partial_{x}^{3}v+\partial_{y}^{3}v=0,\\ v(x,y,0)=v_{0}(x,y),\end{cases}

which, via Fourier transform, is given by V⁡(t)​v0^​(ξ,η)=ei​t​(ξ3+η3)​v^0​(ξ,η)\widehat{V(t)v_{0}}(\xi,\eta)=e^{it(\xi^{3}+\eta^{3})}\widehat{v}_{0}(\xi,\eta).

We now state our main result concerning the existence of dispersive blow-up taking place for the ZK equation.

Theorem 1.1.

Let s∈[1,2)s\in[1,2). There exists

v0∈Hs​(ℝ2)∩C∞​(ℝ2)∩L2​(⟨x⟩r​d​x​d​y),v_{0}\in H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{2})\cap C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})\cap L^{2}(\langle x\rangle^{r}\,dxdy),

for some r>0r>0, so that the solution v⁡(t)v(t) of the IVP (1.2), for k=1k=1, is global in time with

v∈C⁡(ℝ:Hs​(ℝ2))∩…v\in C(\mathbb{R}:H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{2}))\cap\dots

and it satisfies

(1.5) {v(t)∈C1(ℝ2),t>0,t∉ℤ+,v(t)∈C1(ℝ2\(0,0))\C1(ℝ2),t∈ℤ+.\begin{cases}v(t)\in C^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2}),\hskip 79.6678ptt>0,t\notin\mathbb{Z}^{+},\\ v(t)\in C^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash{(0,0)})\backslash C^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2}),\hskip 15.0ptt\in\mathbb{Z}^{+}.\end{cases}

Moreover, if we set

(1.6) z1​(t)=∫0tV⁡(t−t′)​v​(∂xv+∂yv)​(t′)​d​t′,z_{1}(t)=\int_{0}^{t}V(t-t^{\prime})v\left(\partial_{x}v+\partial_{y}v\right)(t^{\prime})\,dt^{\prime},

we have that z1​(t)z_{1}(t) is in C1​(ℝ2)C^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) for any t>0t>0.

Remark 1.1.

This result shows that the dispersive blow-up phenomenon can be established in higher dimensions for nonlinear models with nonlinearities involving derivatives.

In order to prove Theorem 1.1 we first construct an initial data whose linear time evolution fails to be C1​(ℝ2)C^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) at all positive integer times, borrowing some ideas from [29]. Then we show that, even though such a initial data is in H2−​(ℝ2)H^{2^{-}}(\mathbb{R}^{2}), the Duhamel term z1​(t)z_{1}(t) actually is slightly more regular and belongs to H2+​(ℝ2)⊂C1​(ℝ2)H^{2^{+}}(\mathbb{R}^{2})\subset C^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) for any t>0t>0. This smoothing gain in the integral part encapsulates the dispersive blow-up phenomenon as the singularity development is exclusively due to the linear evolution component in (1.3).

To explain our approach we will consider the nonlinear term v​∂xvv\partial_{x}v and then proceed to estimate it along with its derivatives in the xx-variable. To control 2+2^{+} derivatives in xx for z1​(t)z_{1}(t) in the L2L^{2}-norm we will first apply the dual version of the smoothing effect of Kato type (see Lemma 2.3). This allows us to gain 11 derivative but we still end up with the term Dx1+​(v​∂xv)D^{1^{+}}_{x}(v\partial_{x}v) in a Lx1​Ly​T2L^{1}_{x}L^{2}_{yT}-norm. We notice issues are reduced to considering the worst term Dx1+​∂xvD_{x}^{1^{+}}\partial_{x}v but in order to avoid the use of the Lx1L^{1}_{x} norm we must introduce some weights which bring into play the local well-posedness theory for the IVP (1.2) in weighted Sobolev spaces. Recently, Fonseca and Pachon [11] (see also [6]) established the theory in these spaces. Then our next concern is to estimate Dx1+​∂xvD^{1^{+}}_{x}\partial_{x}v. This can be done by using the Strichartz estimates that permit a gain of some extra derivative in the xx-variable. When we analyze the worst term we choose to introduce the commutator [Dx1+,v]​∂xv[D^{1^{+}}_{x},v]\partial_{x}v, which morally is better than the term we have already discussed. Nevertheless this commutator is in the Lx1​Ly​T2L^{1}_{x}L^{2}_{yT}-norm. Again we need to introduce a weight to have this term in LT2​Lx​y2L^{2}_{T}L^{2}_{xy}-norm. At this point we have to appeal to a Kato-Ponce type commutator estimate in weighted spaces proved by Cruz-Uribe and Naibo in [7]. To control the terms after applying the commutator we will use interpolation estimates introduced by Nahas-Ponce [32] and Ponce [33] to distribute weights and derivatives. The key point here is to use Strichartz estimates and avoid Sobolev embedding. This will close the estimates. Same arguments work when we look at the yy-derivatives.

Case k≥2k\geq 2. We observe that the analysis described above can be also used to show a similar result as Theorem 1.1 for solutions of the IVP (1.2) for k≥2k\geq 2. More precisely,

Theorem 1.2.

Let s∈[1,2)s\in[1,2) and k≥2k\geq 2. There exists

v0∈Hs​(ℝ2)∩C∞​(ℝ2)∩L2​(⟨x⟩r​d​x​d​y)v_{0}\in H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{2})\cap C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})\cap L^{2}(\langle x\rangle^{r}\,dxdy)

with ‖v0‖H1≪1\|v_{0}\|_{H^{1}}\ll 1 so that the solution v⁡(t)v(t) of the IVP associated to (1.2) is global in time with

v∈C⁡(ℝ:Hs​(ℝ2))∩…v\in C(\mathbb{R}:H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{2}))\cap\dots

satisfies

{v(t)∈C1(ℝ2),t>0,t∉ℤ+,v(t)∈C1(ℝ2\(0,0))\C1(ℝ2),t∈ℤ+.\begin{cases}v(t)\in C^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2}),\hskip 85.35826ptt>0,t\notin\mathbb{Z}^{+},\\ v(t)\in C^{1}\left(\mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash{(0,0)}\right)\backslash C^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2}),\hskip 15.0ptt\in\mathbb{Z}^{+}.\end{cases}

Since the proof of this result follows by employing a similar analysis as the proof of Theorem 1.1 we will not give the details. We point out, however, the fact that the initial data has small H1H^{1} norm guarantees that the corresponding solution is indeed global in time (see [10] and [25]).

To complete our set of results we consider a generalized kind of dispersive blow-up. We will first show that, given a time t∗≠0t^{*}\neq 0, it is possible to construct an initial data in H1​(ℝ2)∩W1,p​(ℝ2)H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})\cap W^{1,p}(\mathbb{R}^{2}), p>2p>2, such that the solution of the linear problem associated to the gZK equation is not in W1,p​(ℝ2)W^{1,p}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) at time t∗t^{*}. Moreover, we will prove that the solution of the nonlinear problem inherits such a property but this is still provided by the linear part of the solution. The statement will be the first part of our last theorem below.

The second result regards propagation of regularity of solutions of IVP (1.2). In [16] Isaza, Linares and Ponce, considering suitable solutions of the IVP associated to the generalized KdV equation

(1.7) {∂tu+∂x3u+uk​∂xu=0,x,t∈ℝ,k∈ℤ+,u⁡(x,0)=u0​(x),\begin{cases}\partial_{t}u+\partial_{x}^{3}u+u^{k}\partial_{x}u=0,\quad x,t\in\mathbb{R},\;k\in\mathbb{Z}^{+},\\ u(x,0)=u_{0}(x),\end{cases}

Theorem B ([16]).

If u0∈H3/4+​(ℝ)u_{0}\in H^{{3/4}^{+}}(\mathbb{R}) and for some l∈ℤ+,l≥1\,l\in\mathbb{Z}^{+},\,\;l\geq 1, and x0∈ℝx_{0}\in\mathbb{R},

Moreover, for any v≥0v\geq 0, ϵ>0\epsilon>0 and R>0R>0

Our next result complement this last one. More precisely, we will construct initial data in H1​(ℝ2)∩Wr,p​(ℝ2)H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})\cap W^{r,p}(\mathbb{R}^{2}), for some rr and pp, such that the singularities of the solutions do not propagate in any direction. This statement will be the second part of our last theorem below.

We summarize the results described above in the next theorem.

Theorem 1.3.

Fix k≥2k\geq 2.

  1. (1)

    Let t∗≠0t^{*}\neq 0 be a given real number. Then there exists v0∈H1​(ℝ2)∩W1,p​(ℝ2)v_{0}\in H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})\cap W^{1,p}(\mathbb{R}^{2}), p>2p>2, such that the corresponding solution of the IVP (1.2) is global in time and satisfies:

    1. (a)

      v∈C⁡(ℝ:H1​(ℝ2))v\in C(\mathbb{R}:\,H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2}));

      and

    2. (b)

      v⁡(t∗)∉W1,p​(ℝ2)v(t^{*})\notin W^{1,p}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) for every p>2p>2.

  2. (2)

    There exist r>1r>1, p∈(2,10)p\in(2,10), and an initial data v0∈H1​(ℝ2)∩Wr,p​(ℝ2)v_{0}\in H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})\cap W^{r,p}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) such that the corresponding solution of the IVP (1.2) is global in time and satisfies:

    1. (a)

      v∈C⁡(ℝ:H1​(ℝ2))v\in C(\mathbb{R}:\,H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2}));

      and

    2. (b)

      there exists t>0t>0 such that

      v⁡(t)∉Wr,p​(ℝ+2)​ and ​v​(−t)∉Wr,p​(ℝ+2),v(t)\notin W^{r,p}(\mathbb{R}^{2}_{+})\text{\quad and \quad}v(-t)\notin W^{r,p}(\mathbb{R}^{2}_{+}),

      where

      (1.8) ℝ+2:={(x,y)∈ℝ2:y≥0}.\mathbb{R}^{2}_{+}:=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}\;:\;y\geq 0\}.

    The same result holds for ℝ−2:={(x,y)∈ℝ2:y≤0}\mathbb{R}^{2}_{-}:=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}\;:\;y\leq 0\}.

To prove this theorem we extend previous analysis introduced in [23] and [29]. The main ingredient is the smoothness of the Duhamel term as before. In this case we use pure Sobolev spaces, combined with the smoothing effect of Kato type; the main tool being used. More precisely, we have

Proposition 1.4.

Fix k≥2k\geq 2. Let v0∈Hs​(ℝ2)v_{0}\in H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{2}), s=1,2,…s=1,2,\dots, and v∈C⁡([−T,T]:Hs​(ℝ2))v\in C([-T,T]:H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{2})) the local solution of the IVP (1.2). Then

zk​(t)=∫0tV⁡(t−t′)​vk​(∂xv+∂yv)​(t′)​d​t′∈C⁡([−T,T]:Hs+1​(ℝ2)).z_{k}(t)=\int_{0}^{t}V(t-t^{\prime})v^{k}\left(\partial_{x}v+\partial_{y}v\right)(t^{\prime})\,dt^{\prime}\in C([-T,T]:H^{s+1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})).

The argument to prove Proposition 1.4 employs the smoothing properties of solutions of the linear problem and the properties of the solution of the IVP itself. We will give the details only for the case k=2k=2. For the other nonlinearities we shall follow the arguments given here and those in [25] where the local theory for the IVP (1.1) is established in Hs​(ℝ2)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{2}), for s>s0s>s_{0}, 0<s0<10<s_{0}<1. This latter result implies global well-posedness of the IVP in Hs​(ℝ2)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{2}), s≥1s\geq 1, whenever the initial data are small enough.

The paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 we recall estimates and results for the linear and nonlinear ZK and gZK equations, that will be needed in the proofs that follow. In Section 3 we construct the smooth initial data whose linear evolution develops singularities at all future integer times and which embodies the dispersive blow-up phenomenon. In Section 4 we prove the nonlinear smoothing effect for the ZK equation (k=1k=1), which in this particular case consists in showing that for initial data in H2−​(ℝ2)H^{2^{-}}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) the Duhamel term corresponding to the nonlinear evolution is actually slightly more regular, it belongs to H2+​(ℝ2)H^{2^{+}}(\mathbb{R}^{2}). Finally, in Section 5 we prove Theorem 1.3 and Proposition 1.4.

5. Proof of nonlinear smoothing for k=2k=2

We now consider solutions of the IVP associated to the modified Zakharov-Kuznetsov equation,

(5.1) {∂tu+∂x3u+∂y3u+u2(∂xu+∂yu)=0,(x,y)∈ℝ2,t∈ℝ,u⁡(x,y,0)=u0​(x,y).\begin{cases}\partial_{t}u+\partial_{x}^{3}u+\partial_{y}^{3}u+u^{2}(\partial_{x}u+\partial_{y}u)=0,\hskip 15.0pt(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{2},\;t\in\mathbb{R},\\ u(x,y,0)=u_{0}(x,y).\end{cases}

In this section we show that we can obtain the nonlinear smoothing effect of the Duhamel term of the solution without using weighted Sobolev spaces. We start by giving the local well-posedness result that we will use in this case.

and

Moreover, for any T′∈(0,T)T^{\prime}\in(0,T) there exists a neighborhood 𝒲\mathcal{W} of u0∈Hs​(ℝ2)u_{0}\in H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) such that the map u~0↦u~​(t)\tilde{u}_{0}\mapsto\tilde{u}(t) from 𝒲\mathcal{W} into the the class defined by (5.2)–(5.5), with T′T^{\prime} instead of TT, is Lipschitz.

The proof relies on the contraction mapping principle and it is quite similar to that of Theorem 1.1 in [25]. The Strichartz estimates in Corollary 2.2, Kato’s smoothing effects in Lemma 2.3 combined with the maximal function estimate in Lemma 2.4 are enough to recover the loss of derivatives in the nonlinear term of (5.1). ∎

Since ϕ∈H1​(ℝ2)∩W1,1​(ℝ2)\phi\in H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})\cap W^{1,1}(\mathbb{R}^{2}), an interpolation using (5.14) and (5.15) gives that V⁡(t)​∂xϕ∈Lp​(ℝ2)V(t)\partial_{x}\phi\in L^{p}(\mathbb{R}^{2}), for any p≥2p\geq 2. Similar estimates hold if we replace ∂xϕ\partial_{x}\phi by ϕ\phi or ∂yϕ\partial_{y}\phi in (5.14) and (5.15), from which we deduce that V⁡(t)​ϕ∈W1,p​(ℝ2)V(t)\phi\in W^{1,p}(\mathbb{R}^{2}), for any p≥2p\geq 2 and each t≠0t\neq 0.

Next we choose v0​(x,y)=V⁡(−t∗)​ϕ​(x,y)v_{0}(x,y)=V(-t^{*})\phi(x,y). Multiplying v0v_{0} by a small constant, if necessary, we may assume that the corresponding solution, say, v⁡(t)v(t), is global in time with v∈C⁡(ℝ:H1​(ℝ2))v\in C(\mathbb{R}:H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})). Since V⁡(t∗)V(t^{*}) is a unitary group in H1​(ℝ2)H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) we deduce that v0∈H1​(ℝ2)∩W1,p​(ℝ2)v_{0}\in H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})\cap W^{1,p}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) with V⁡(t∗)​v0=ϕ∈H1​(ℝ2)V(t^{*})v_{0}=\phi\in H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) but ϕ∉W1,p​(ℝ2)\phi\notin W^{1,p}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) for every p>2p>2. This implies claim (1).

Next we prove part (2). First we note that by taking ε=1/2\varepsilon=1/2 and θ∈[0,1)\theta\in[0,1) in Lemma 2.1, we have, for p>2p>2,

(5.16) ‖Dxp−24​p​V​(t)​v0‖Lt12​p5​(p−2)​Lx​yp≤c​‖v0‖Lx​y2\|D^{\frac{p-2}{4p}}_{x}V(t)v_{0}\|_{L^{\frac{12p}{5(p-2)}}_{t}L^{p}_{xy}}\leq c\|v_{0}\|_{L^{2}_{xy}}

and

(5.17) ‖Dyp−24​p​V​(t)​v0‖Lt12​p5​(p−2)​Lx​yp≤c​‖v0‖Lx​y2,\|D^{\frac{p-2}{4p}}_{y}V(t)v_{0}\|_{L^{\frac{12p}{5(p-2)}}_{t}L^{p}_{xy}}\leq c\|v_{0}\|_{L^{2}_{xy}},

for any v0∈L2​(ℝ2)v_{0}\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2}).

We take v~0∈H1​(ℝ2)\widetilde{v}_{0}\in H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) with 1=r−p−24​p=r−p^1=r-\frac{p-2}{4p}=r-\hat{p} with v~0∉Wr,p​(ℝ+2)\widetilde{v}_{0}\notin W^{r,p}(\mathbb{R}^{2}_{+}), where ℝ+2\mathbb{R}^{2}_{+} is defined as (1.8). From (5.16) and (5.17) there exists t~>0\tilde{t}>0 such that

V⁡(±t~)​v~0,V⁡(±2​t~)​v~0∈Wr,p​(ℝ2)with​r=1+p−24​p=j.V(\pm\tilde{t}\,)\widetilde{v}_{0},\quad V(\pm 2\tilde{t}\,)\widetilde{v}_{0}\in W^{r,p}(\mathbb{R}^{2})\quad\text{with}\;\;r=1+\frac{p-2}{4p}=j.

Next we consider the initial data

(5.18) v0=V⁡(t~)​v~0+V⁡(−t~)​v~0.v_{0}=V(\tilde{t}\,)\widetilde{v}_{0}+V(-\tilde{t}\,)\widetilde{v}_{0}.

We observe that v0∈H1​(ℝ2)∩Wr,p​(ℝ2)v_{0}\in H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})\cap W^{r,p}(\mathbb{R}^{2}). In addition, multiplying v0v_{0} by a small constant, if necessary, we may also assume that the corresponding solution is global in time with v∈C⁡(ℝ:H1​(ℝ2))v\in C(\mathbb{R}:H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})). On the other hand, we have from Proposition 1.4 that zk​(t)∈C⁡([−T,T]:H2​(ℝ2))z_{k}(t)\in C([-T,T]:H^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})). Hence, the Sobolev embedding implies that

C⁡([−T,T]:H2​(ℝ2))↪C⁡([−T,T]:Wr,p​(ℝ2))C([-T,T]:H^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2}))\hookrightarrow C([-T,T]:W^{r,p}(\mathbb{R}^{2}))

whenever p∈(2,10)p\in(2,10).

We finally note that

V⁡(t~)​v0=V⁡(2​t~)​v~0+v~0∉Wr,p​(ℝ+2)V(\tilde{t}\,)v_{0}=V(2\tilde{t}\,)\widetilde{v}_{0}+\widetilde{v}_{0}\notin W^{r,p}(\mathbb{R}^{2}_{+})

and the same holds for V⁡(−t~)​v0V(-\tilde{t}\,)v_{0}.

Combining the above information we derive the desired result. ∎
